claim: RtcB enzymes are RNA ligases that play essential roles in tRNA splicing, unfolded protein response, and RNA repair.
source: RtcB enzymes are RNA ligases that play essential roles in tRNA splicing, unfolded protein response, and RNA repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these roles.

claim: In metazoa, RtcB functions as part of a five-subunit tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC) along with Ddx1, Cgi-99, Fam98B, and Ashwin.
source: In metazoa, RtcB functions as part of a five-subunit tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC) along with Ddx1, Cgi-99, Fam98B, and Ashwin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is consistent with established knowledge about the tRNA-LC composition.

claim: The human tRNA-LC or its individual subunits have been implicated in additional cellular processes including microRNA maturation, viral replication, DNA double-strand break repair, and mRNA transport.
source: The human tRNA-LC or its individual subunits have been implicated in additional cellular processes including microRNA maturation, viral replication, DNA double-strand break repair, and mRNA transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The core of the human tRNA-LC is assembled from RTCB and the C-terminal alpha-helical regions of DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B, all of which are required for complex integrity.
source: We show that the core of the human tRNA-LC is assembled from RTCB and the C-terminal alpha-helical regions of DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B, all of which are required for complex integrity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deletion analysis and truncation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 displays structural homology to calponin-homology domains.
source: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 displays structural homology to calponin-homology domains
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and structural comparison analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CGI-99 and FAM98B associate via their N-terminal domains to form a stable subcomplex.
source: CGI-99 and FAM98B associate via their N-terminal domains to form a stable subcomplex.
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of GMP-bound RTCB reveals divalent metal coordination geometry in the active site.
source: The crystal structure of GMP-bound RTCB reveals divalent metal coordination geometry in the active site, providing insights into its catalytic mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Canonical ligases are ATP-dependent enzymes that catalyze the formation of a 3′,5′-phosphodiester linkage between 3′-hydroxyl (3′-OH) and 5′-phosphate (5′-P) RNA termini.
source: Canonical ligases, including bacteriophage T4 RNA ligase 1 or Saccharomyces cerevisiae tRNA ligase Trl1, are ATP-dependent enzymes that catalyze the formation of a 3′,5′-phosphodiester linkage between 3′-hydroxyl (3′-OH) and 5′-phosphate (5′-P) RNA termini (Banerjee et al., 2019; El Omari et al., 2006; Greer et al., 1983; Gu et al., 2016; Nandakumar et al., 2006; Peebles et al., 1979; Peschek and Walter, 2019; Unciuleac et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: RtcB ligases are GTP-dependent enzymes that catalyze the direct joining of RNA strands with terminal 2′,3′>P and 5′-OH.
source: By contrast, the RtcB ligases are GTP-dependent enzymes that catalyze the direct joining of RNA strands with terminal 2′,3′>P and 5′-OH (Chakravarty et al., 2012; Tanaka and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RtcB ligases incorporate the substrate-derived 2′,3′>P into the resulting 3′,5′-phosphodiester bond.
source: In contrast to the mechanism of canonical RNA ligases, in which the source of the splice-junction phosphate group is the ATP cofactor, RtcB ligases incorporate the substrate-derived 2′,3′>P into the resulting 3′,5′-phosphodiester bond (Filipowicz and Shatkin, 1983; Popow et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RtcB ligases are present throughout all domains of life with notable absences in plants and some fungi, including the model organisms S. cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: RtcB ligases are present throughout all domains of life with notable absences in plants and some fungi, including the model organisms S. cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Dantuluri et al., 2021; Popow et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In archaea and eukaryotes, RtcB enzymes catalyze the ligation of tRNA exon halves to produce mature tRNAs upon cleavage of precursor tRNA transcripts by the tRNA splicing endonuclease.
source: In archaea and eukaryotes, RtcB enzymes catalyze the ligation of tRNA exon halves to produce mature tRNAs upon cleavage of precursor tRNA transcripts by the tRNA splicing endonuclease (Calvin and Li, 2008; Li et al., 1998; Peebles et al., 1983; Trotta et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, RtcB ligases function as part of the UPR to catalyze splicing of XBP1 mRNA after its stress-induced cleavage by IRE1.
source: Furthermore, in eukaryotes, RtcB ligases also function as part of the UPR to catalyze splicing of XBP1 mRNA after its stress-induced cleavage by IRE1 (inositol-requiring enzyme 1) (Jurkin et al., 2014; Kosmaczewski et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacterial RtcB ligases are nonessential enzymes involved in RNA repair.
source: In turn, bacterial RtcB ligases are nonessential enzymes involved in RNA repair, for example, during rescue of ribosomal RNAs cleaved by the MazF ribonuclease of the MazE-MazF toxin-antitoxin system activated upon stress (Manwar et al., 2020; Temmel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The RNA ligation mechanism of RtcB enzymes consists of three nucleotidyl transfer steps.
source: The RNA ligation mechanism of RtcB enzymes consists of three nucleotidyl transfer steps.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the mechanism.

claim: In the first step of RtcB ligation, a nucleophilic attack of an invariant histidine residue in the active site on the α-phosphate moiety of GTP results in a covalently linked RtcB-GMP intermediate with the concomitant release of inorganic pyrophosphate.
source: First, a nucleophilic attack of an invariant histidine residue in the active site (His428 in human RTCB, His404 in Pyrococcus horikoshii RtcB, PhRtcB, and His337 in Escherichia coli RtcB, EcRtcB) on the α-phosphate moiety of guanine-5′-triphosphate (GTP) results in a covalently linked RtcB-GMP intermediate with the concomitant release of inorganic pyrophosphate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the mechanism.

claim: In the second step of RtcB ligation, the terminal 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate of the 5′ exon is hydrolyzed to 3′-phosphate, which subsequently carries out a nucleophilic attack on the phosphate group of RtcB-GMP conjugate to form an activated RNA-(3′)pp(5′)G intermediate.
source: Second, the terminal 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate of the 5′ exon is hydrolyzed to 3′-phosphate, which subsequently carries out a nucleophilic attack on the phosphate group of RtcB-GMP conjugate to form an activated RNA-(3′)pp(5′)G intermediate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the mechanism.

claim: In the final step of RtcB ligation, the activated 3′ end of the 5′ exon undergoes nucleophilic attack by the 5′-OH of the 3′ exon, resulting in exon ligation and release of GMP.
source: Finally, the activated 3′ end of the 5′ exon undergoes nucleophilic attack by the 5′-OH of the 3′ exon, resulting in exon ligation and release of GMP (Chakravarty and Shuman, 2012; Chakravarty et al., 2012; Desai et al., 2013; Englert et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the mechanism.

claim: The ligation reaction of RtcB enzymes is dependent on the presence of divalent metal ions.
source: The ligation reaction of RtcB enzymes is dependent on the presence of divalent metal ions, consistent with the observation of two active site-bound Mn2+ ions in the crystal structures of PhRtcB (Das et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2011; Tanaka and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some RtcB orthologs, including human RTCB and PhRtcB, require Archease, a dedicated protein cofactor that facilitates the initial guanylation of RtcB and promotes its multiple turnover.
source: Some RtcB orthologs, including human RTCB and PhRtcB, require Archease, a dedicated protein cofactor that facilitates the initial guanylation of RtcB and promotes its multiple turnover (Desai et al., 2014; Popow et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The catalytic activity of human RTCB is sensitive to copper-mediated oxidative inactivation under aerobic conditions.
source: The catalytic activity of human RTCB was recently shown to be sensitive to copper-mediated oxidative inactivation under aerobic conditions (Asanović et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The oxidoreductase PYROXD1 protects the active site of RTCB by forming a complex with RTCB in the presence of NAD(P)H.
source: The inactivation is counteracted by the oxidoreductase PYROXD1, which protects the active site of RTCB by forming a complex with RTCB in the presence of NAD(P)H (Asanović et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The human RtcB ligase ortholog RTCB is part of an essential heteropentameric tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC), along with the DEAD-box helicase DDX1, as well as FAM98B, CGI-99, and ASHWIN.
source: The human RtcB ligase ortholog RTCB, also referred to as HSPC117 or FAAP, is part of an essential heteropentameric tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC), along with the DEAD-box helicase DDX1, as well as FAM98B, CGI-99 (also known as RTRAF or hCLE), and ASHWIN (ASW) (Popow et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RTCB is the only subunit of tRNA-LC that is essential and sufficient for RNA ligation.
source: RTCB is the only subunit of tRNA-LC that is essential and sufficient for RNA ligation, but it requires the protein cofactor Archease for multiple-turnover catalysis (Popow et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 enhances the RTCB-catalyzed RNA ligation via its RNA-dependent ATPase activity.
source: DDX1 enhances the RTCB-catalyzed RNA ligation via its RNA-dependent ATPase activity (Popow et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in DNA double-strand break repair.
source: but it is also involved in other cellular processes including DNA double-strand break repair (Li et al., 2016; Li et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in microRNA maturation.
source: microRNA maturation (Han et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in regulation of insulin translation.
source: regulation of insulin translation (Li et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in regulation of viral replication including HIV-1.
source: or regulation of viral replication including HIV-1 (Edgcomb et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in regulation of foot-and-mouth disease virus replication.
source: foot-and-mouth disease virus (Xue et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in regulation of infectious bronchitis virus replication.
source: infectious bronchitis virus (Xu et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in regulation of SARS-CoV-2 replication.
source: and SARS-CoV-2 (Kamel et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CGI-99, FAM98B, and ASW have no effect on the RNA ligation activity of tRNA-LC.
source: While CGI-99, FAM98B, and ASW have no effect on the RNA ligation activity of tRNA-LC (Popow et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CGI-99 functions as a transcription modulator in viral replication.
source: CGI-99 was shown to function as a transcription modulator in viral replication (Huarte et al., 2001; Rodriguez-Frandsen et al., 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A stable, catalytically active complex could be obtained by coexpression of all five subunits (RTCB, DDX1, FAM98B, CGI-99, and ASW) and affinity purification.
source: A stable, catalytically active complex could be obtained by coexpression of all five subunits and affinity purification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Deletion of any of RTCB, DDX1, FAM98B, or CGI-99 resulted in failure of the remaining four subunits to form a stable complex.
source: Affinity purifications from insect cells infected with expression constructs lacking one of the subunits revealed that deletion of any of RTCB, DDX1, FAM98B, or CGI-99 resulted in failure of the remaining four subunits to form a stable complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ASW could be omitted without compromising complex assembly.
source: Only ASW, a 26 kDa, intrinsically disordered protein with no conserved domains other than a leucine-rich region and two nuclear localization signals (Patil et al., 2006), could be omitted without compromising complex assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deletion analysis and a citation to prior literature about ASW structure.

claim: The integrity of tRNA-LC is dependent on the simultaneous presence of RTCB, DDX1, FAM98B, and CGI-99.
source: These results indicate that the integrity of tRNA-LC is dependent on the simultaneous presence of RTCB, DDX1, FAM98B, and CGI-99, suggesting that these subunits form a stable core of tRNA-LC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the deletion analysis experimental data.

claim: DDX1, FAM98B, and CGI-99 display similar phylogenetic distribution.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the evolutionary conservation of tRNA-LC subunits, whereas DDX1, FAM98B, and CGI-99 display similar phylogenetic distribution
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASW is absent from many organisms where the other subunits of tRNA-LC are present.
source: ASW is absent from many organisms where the other subunits of tRNA-LC are present (Popow et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of either DDX1 or RTCB, ASW forms a complex together with CGI-99 and FAM98B, but not with either of these subunits alone.
source: Furthermore, affinity purifications of MBP-tagged ASW or StrepII-tagged CGI-99 revealed that in the absence of either DDX1 or RTCB, ASW forms a complex together with CGI-99 and FAM98B, but not with either of these subunits alone (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CGI-99 and FAM98B were able to form a stable subcomplex in the absence of all other tRNA-LC subunits.
source: Additionally, CGI-99 and FAM98B were able to form a stable subcomplex in the absence of all other tRNA-LC subunits (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The interaction of ASW with tRNA-LC is dependent on the CGI-99:FAM98B subcomplex and is likely mediated through the CGI-99:FAM98B interface.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the interaction of ASW with tRNA-LC is dependent on the CGI-99:FAM98B subcomplex and is likely mediated through the CGI-99:FAM98B interface.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on subunit interactions.

claim: RTCB binds Archease with nanomolar affinity.
source: Although RTCB binds Archease with nanomolar affinity, Archease does not co-purify with RTCB when the latter is affinity-purified from HEK293 cells (Popow et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Archease does not co-purify with RTCB when the latter is affinity-purified from HEK293 cells.
source: Although RTCB binds Archease with nanomolar affinity, Archease does not co-purify with RTCB when the latter is affinity-purified from HEK293 cells (Popow et al., 2014), suggesting that Archease only transiently interacts with the tRNA-LC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Archease does not form a stable complex with the tRNA-LC in vitro.
source: In agreement with previous studies, tRNA-LC and Archease eluted in separate peaks, indicating that Archease does not form a stable complex with the tRNA-LC in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography analysis.

claim: 103 or 143 validated intra-subunit cross-links were identified for the five-subunit full complex in two experimental replicates.
source: Analyzing two experimental replicates for each complex, we identified 103 or 143 validated intra-subunit and 104 or 141 validated inter-subunit cross-links for the five-subunit full complex
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: 104 or 141 validated inter-subunit cross-links were identified for the five-subunit full complex in two experimental replicates.
source: Analyzing two experimental replicates for each complex, we identified 103 or 143 validated intra-subunit and 104 or 141 validated inter-subunit cross-links for the five-subunit full complex
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: 156 or 146 validated intra-subunit cross-links were identified for the four-subunit core complex in two experimental replicates.
source: and 156 or 146 validated intra-subunit and 102 or 92 validated inter-subunit cross-links for the four-subunit core complex (with a false discovery rate of <5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: 102 or 92 validated inter-subunit cross-links were identified for the four-subunit core complex in two experimental replicates.
source: and 156 or 146 validated intra-subunit and 102 or 92 validated inter-subunit cross-links for the four-subunit core complex (with a false discovery rate of <5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: 66 of the inter-subunit cross-links involving RTCB, DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B were detected in both the four-subunit and five-subunit complex samples.
source: 66 of the inter-subunit cross-links involving RTCB, DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B were detected in both the four-subunit and five-subunit complex samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: The C-terminal region of DDX1 formed numerous cross-links with the remaining subunits of the five-subunit complex, with the exception of FAM98B.
source: The C-terminal region of DDX1 formed numerous cross-links with the remaining subunits of the five-subunit complex, with the exception of FAM98B, suggesting that the interaction of DDX1 with the remaining subunits within tRNA-LC is mediated by the C-terminal region (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The interaction of DDX1 with the remaining subunits within tRNA-LC is mediated by the C-terminal region.
source: The C-terminal region of DDX1 formed numerous cross-links with the remaining subunits of the five-subunit complex, with the exception of FAM98B, suggesting that the interaction of DDX1 with the remaining subunits within tRNA-LC is mediated by the C-terminal region (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: For RTCB and FAM98B, the cross-links mapped mostly to their respective C-terminal regions.
source: For RTCB and FAM98B, the cross-links also mapped mostly to their respective C-terminal regions
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: CGI-99 cross-links were spread throughout its primary structure.
source: while CGI-99 cross-links were spread throughout its primary structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: ASW formed cross-links with all remaining subunits, particularly via its N-terminal region.
source: ASW formed cross-links with all remaining subunits, particularly via its N-terminal region.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: A notable reduction of cross-links between the C-terminal regions of DDX1 and FAM98B was observed in the five-subunit full complex as compared to the four-subunit core complex.
source: A notable reduction of cross-links between the C-terminal regions of DDX1 and FAM98B was observed in the five-subunit full complex (Figure 2A) as compared to the four-subunit core complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ASW is positioned between DDX1 and FAM98B or modulates their conformations.
source: suggesting that ASW is positioned between DDX1 and FAM98B or modulates their conformations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claim: Both CGI-99 and FAM98B comprise N-terminal calponin homology (CH)-like domains followed by putative C-terminal coiled-coil regions.
source: Structural modeling using Phyre2 (Kelley et al., 2015) and PCOILS (Lupas et al., 1991) servers predicted that both CGI-99 and FAM98B comprised N-terminal calponin homology (CH)-like domains followed by putative C-terminal coiled-coil regions (Figure 1A; Schou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling predictions and citations to prior literature.

claim: The crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 comprising residues Phe2-Asp101 was determined at a resolution of 2.0 Å.
source: To verify this experimentally, we determined the crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 comprising residues Phe2-Asp101CGI-99 at a resolution of 2.0 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 adopts a globular fold connected via a flexible linker to an N-terminal α-helix comprising residues Phe2–Asn18.
source: The protein construct adopts a globular fold connected via a flexible linker to an N-terminal α-helix comprising residues Phe2–Asn18CGI-99, which is stabilized in different conformations in the two molecules present in the asymmetric unit by crystal packing interactions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The closest structural homologs of the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 include the CH domains of the human kinetochore protein NDC80 (PDB ID: 2ve7, rmsd of 3.6 Å over 74 Cα atoms).
source: The closest structural homologs identified by the DALI server (Holm, 2020) include the CH domains of the human kinetochore protein NDC80 (PDB ID: 2ve7, root mean square deviation [rmsd] of 3.6 Å over 74 Cα atoms)
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis using the DALI server.

claim: The closest structural homologs of the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 include the Chlamydomonas reinhardtii intraflagellar transport protein IFT54 (PDB ID: 5fmt, rmsd 3.1 Å over 71 Cα atoms).
source: and the Chlamydomonas reinhardtii intraflagellar transport protein IFT54 (PDB ID: 5fmt, rmsd 3.1 Å over 71 Cα atoms) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis using the DALI server.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 exhibits close structural homology with the helical N-terminal domain of E. coli Lon protease (PDB ID: 3ljc, rmsd 2.7 Å over 80 Cα atoms).
source: However, the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 also exhibits close structural homology with non-CH domains such as the helical N-terminal domain of E. coli Lon protease (PDB ID: 3ljc, rmsd 2.7 Å over 80 Cα atoms) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 adopts a calponin homology-like fold.
source: Together, these observations confirm that the N-terminal domain of CGI-99 adopts a calponin homology-like fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis.

claim: The overall level of overexpressed FAM98B was reduced in the absence of CGI-99.
source: Interestingly, the overall level of overexpressed FAM98B was reduced in the absence of CGI-99, indicating that CGI-99 has a stabilizing effect on FAM98B in the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from pull-down assays.

claim: CGI-99 has a stabilizing effect on FAM98B in the cell.
source: Interestingly, the overall level of overexpressed FAM98B was reduced in the absence of CGI-99, indicating that CGI-99 has a stabilizing effect on FAM98B in the cell.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 (Phe2-Asp101) was able to co-precipitate a minimal FAM98B construct spanning residues Arg2-Lys184.
source: The N-terminal domain of CGI-99 (Phe2-Asp101CGI-99) was able to co-precipitate a minimal FAM98B construct spanning residues Arg2-Lys184FAM98B (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The CGI-99:FAM98B interaction is dependent on both the N-terminal CH domain and a predicted beta-hairpin motif (residues Glu145-Lys184) in FAM98B, and the N-terminal CH domain in CGI-99.
source: indicating that the CGI-99:FAM98B interaction is dependent on both the N-terminal CH domain and a predicted beta-hairpin motif (residues Glu145-Lys184FAM98B) in FAM98B, and the N-terminal CH domain in CGI-99.
evidence: This claim is inferred from pull-down assay data.

claim: The putative C-terminal coiled-coil regions of CGI-99 and FAM98B were dispensable for the interaction.
source: In contrast, the putative C-terminal coiled-coil regions of CGI-99 and FAM98B were dispensable for the interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The formation of the CGI-99:FAM98B heterodimer is mediated by the respective N-terminal regions of the subunits.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the formation of the CGI-99:FAM98B heterodimer is mediated by the respective N-terminal regions of the subunits
evidence: This claim is inferred from pull-down assay data.

claim: The N-terminal CH-like domains of CGI-99 and FAM98B may comprise an independently functioning module within tRNA-LC.
source: and suggest that the N-terminal CH-like domains of CGI-99 and FAM98B may comprise an independently functioning module within tRNA-LC.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the experimental data.

claim: DDX1 is an 82 kDa DEAD-box helicase comprising two canonical RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), an atypical SPRY domain inserted in the N-terminal RecA1 domain and a C-terminal extension.
source: DDX1 is an 82 kDa DEAD-box helicase comprising two canonical RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), an atypical SPRY domain inserted in the N-terminal RecA1 domain and a C-terminal extension (Figure 1A; Kellner and Meinhart, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is consistent with Figure 1A.

claim: The C-terminal region of DDX1, comprising the RecA2 domain and the C-terminal extension, is sufficient to support tRNA-LC assembly.
source: Following affinity purification, SEC analysis confirmed integrity of the complex, indicating that the C-terminal region of DDX1, comprising the RecA2 domain and the C-terminal extension, is sufficient to support tRNA-LC assembly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MS analysis of fragments separated by SEC revealed DDX1 cleavage, resulting in the loss of a fragment spanning residues Ser436-Arg694 corresponding to the RecA2 domain.
source: MS analysis of fragments separated by SEC revealed DDX1 cleavage, resulting in the loss of a fragment spanning residues Ser436-Arg694DDX1 corresponding to the RecA2 domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The C-terminal extension of DDX1, corresponding to residues Ala695-Phe740, is sufficient to mediate tRNA-LC assembly.
source: In light of the previously demonstrated requirement of DDX1 for tRNA-LC integrity, this result implies that the C-terminal extension of DDX1, corresponding to residues Ala695-Phe740DDX1, is sufficient to mediate tRNA-LC assembly.
evidence: This claim is inferred from limited proteolysis and mass spectrometry data.

claim: A minimal fragment of DDX1 corresponding to the C-terminal extension (residues Ala696-Phe740) was sufficient for the assembly of the four-subunit core tRNA-LC.
source: Co-precipitation experiments revealed that a minimal fragment of DDX1 corresponding to the C-terminal extension (residues Ala696-Phe740DDX1) was sufficient for the assembly of the four-subunit core tRNA-LC.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-precipitation experimental data.

claim: Neither a shorter C-terminal DDX1 construct (residues Leu729-Phe740) nor a DDX1 construct containing the RecA1 and RecA2 domains but lacking the C-terminal extension (residues Ala2-Ala695) were able to support tRNA-LC assembly.
source: In contrast, neither a shorter C-terminal DDX1 construct (residues Leu729-Phe740DDX1) nor a DDX1 construct containing the RecA1 and RecA2 domains but lacking the C-terminal extension (residues Ala2-Ala695DDX1) were able to support tRNA-LC assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-precipitation experimental data.

claim: The N-terminal domains of CGI-99 and FAM98B, although sufficient for the CGI-99:FAM98B interaction, were dispensable for tRNA-LC assembly.
source: For both CGI-99 and FAM98B, we observed that their N-terminal domains, although sufficient for the CGI-99:FAM98B interaction (Figure 3C), were dispensable for tRNA-LC assembly (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by truncation analysis data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: A CGI-99 fragment spanning residues Ala195-Asp232 was essential and sufficient for the formation of the core complex.
source: Instead, a CGI-99 fragment spanning residues Ala195-Asp232CGI-99 was essential and sufficient for the formation of the core complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by truncation analysis data.

claim: The minimal region of FAM98B that was essential and sufficient for tRNA-LC assembly spans residues Asn200-Ser239.
source: The minimal region of FAM98B that was essential and sufficient for tRNA-LC assembly could be mapped to a region spanning residues Asn200-Ser239FAM98B.
evidence: This claim is supported by truncation analysis data.

claim: A fragment of CGI-99 comprising residues Leu102-Arg244 was necessary for the assembly of the minimal complex, as opposed to a shorter fragment (Ala195-Asp232) sufficient for complex assembly when DDX1 and FAM98B were full-length.

claim: The structural core of tRNA-LC is composed of RTCB together with the C-terminal alpha-helical regions of DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B.

claim: DDX1, CGI-99, and FAM98B interact synergistically to form a structural platform that interacts with the catalytic domain of the RTCB ligase subunit.

claim: The activity of the complex was not increased in the presence of ATP.

claim: The RNA-dependent ATPase activity of DDX1 is not involved in ligase inhibition.

claim: Two adjacent loops found in the vicinity of the active site in RTCB are structurally distinct from PhRtcB: an N-terminal region spanning residues Leu45-Pro64 and a segment comprising residues Arg436-Asp444.

claim: The N-terminal extension of human RTCB is not essential for the formation of tRNA-LC.
